input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

output:
We conducted controlled generation experiments to compare the proposed graph-guided prompting pipeline with a baseline linear prompting workflow. Below we describe, in reproducible terms, the intended experimental setup and the datasets used; where implementation particulars (catalog identifiers, hardware logs, random seeds, and raw prompts) are not yet available in this draft, we explicitly list them as items to attach in the final manuscript or supplementary materials.

Datasets and topical domains
- Domains: Experiments target two topical domains selected to exercise different evidence-retrieval characteristics and sectioning patterns (hereafter referred to as Domain A and Domain B). The precise topical labels and rationales for their selection will be supplied in the final manuscript.
- Data sources: Per the project scope, generation inputs derive from (a) internal author notes and (b) a small curated set of PDFs (paper- and report‑style documents) used as the retrieval corpus when available. These source categories were chosen to reflect realistic author-provided seeds and a limited external evidence pool typical in constrained drafting scenarios.
- Document partitioning: For each domain, the corpus was partitioned into (i) an evidence index for retrieval, (ii) a small set of exemplar documents used for prompt examples where applicable, and (iii) a held-out set used only for manual audit and annotation of unsupported assertions. Exact document identifiers, counts, and provenance records will be included in supplementary material to support reproducibility.

Comparator and pipeline variants
- Baseline (linear prompting): The baseline pipeline follows a conventional left-to-right section generation strategy in which section texts are produced sequentially using prompts that include local context and any retrieved evidence for that section. Outputs are constrained to the same JSON schema used across conditions to ensure comparable post-processing and validation.
- Graph-guided pipeline (proposed): The experimental condition implements the document/section graph construction, leaf-first scheduling, and evidence-injection protocol described in Methods. Key differences from the baseline are (i) an explicit section dependency graph that determines generation order, (ii) retrieval queries augmented with dependency-derived context (e.g., parentsection hypotheses and sibling constraints), and (iii) stronger prompt scaffolding to enforce citation placement and JSON-structured outputs.
- Variants: Where relevant, we evaluate ablations that isolate the impact of (a) scheduling (leaf-first vs. linear order), (b) evidence-injection (prompted evidence vs. no evidence), and (c) JSON-constraining (strict schema enforcement vs. soft instruction). These variants are intended to attribute observed differences to specific components of the proposed workflow.

Generation protocol and application of scheduling/evidence injection
- Section-graph scheduling: For each target document, we construct a section graph encoding parent–child relations and precedence edges (e.g., Methods precedes Results when Results depends on Methods outputs). The scheduler produces a leaf-first order so that sections with minimal downstream dependencies and strong retrieval signal are generated first. During generation, completed sections are appended to a shared context store and used as soft context (not definitive evidence) for dependent sections.
- Evidence retrieval and injection per section: For each scheduled section, the system formulates retrieval queries derived from (i) the section title and intent, (ii) the current section graph neighborhood (parents and children), and (iii) available author notes for that section. Top-ranked evidence items, together with provenance metadata (document id, page/paragraph offsets), are injected into the generation prompt in a standardized evidence block; prompts also require the model to cite injected items when asserting factual content.
- JSON-constrained outputs: Prompts instruct the model to emit section outputs strictly adhering to a machine-readable JSON schema (fields for ``text'', ``citations'', ``summary'', and optional ``warnings'' or ``failure_reasons''). Generated JSON is parsed and validated automatically; failures trigger deterministic repair attempts (e.g., re-request generation with relaxed temperature or a clarification prompt) or are flagged for manual review. All outputs retain provenance links between cited assertions and the original evidence items.
- Logging and audit trails: The pipeline records prompt templates, injected evidence identifiers, model temperature/settings, and validation outcomes for each generation step. These logs enable later audit and targeted post-hoc corrections.

Runtime details and reproducibility artifacts (to be attached)
- Model and API details: The specific language model(s), versions, and API endpoints used for generation will be listed in the final report. For reproducibility we capture model config (temperature, top-k/top-p), token limits, and any post-processing code versions.
- Prompt variants and seeds: Full prompt text for each condition and all random seeds used for sampling will be published in the supplement.
- Hardware and software: Execution environment (CPU/GPU types, memory), container images or environment.yml/requirements.txt, and wall-clock runtimes per document will be provided.
- Evaluation splits and annotation protocol: Annotator guidelines, inter-annotator agreement statistics, and the exact held-out audit set identifiers will be provided.

Annotation and measurement workflows
- Unsupported assertions and citation coverage are assessed via manual annotation on the held-out audit set: each factual claim in generated text is tagged as supported by an injected evidence item, supported by external (non-injected) evidence, or unsupported. Annotation guidelines and examples will be included externally.
- Reviewer-style scoring is obtained from blinded annotators who rate sections on factuality, coherence, and citation appropriateness using a predefined rubric. The rubric and rater training materials will be released with the paper's supplementary assets.

Limitations and missing implementation specifics
- This section intentionally omits domain labels, concrete dataset identifiers, and low-level run logs because those artifacts are not yet attached to this draft. To finalize the experimental section we request the following items for inclusion in the appendix or a reproducibility repository:
  1. Exact topical domain names and justification for their selection.
  2. Document identifiers and provenance for the internal notes and curated PDF corpus.
  3. Model names/versions and API configurations.
  4. Prompt templates for all experimental conditions and ablations.
  5. Random seeds, hardware specifications, and wall-clock runtimes.
  6. Annotation guidelines, sample annotations, and inter-annotator agreement statistics.

Concluding remark
- The experimental setup is organized to isolate the effects of graph-aware scheduling and evidence-aware prompting while preserving a common evaluation scaffold (JSON outputs and manual audit). Final numerical details and reproducibility assets will be appended once the listed artifacts are provided.
